blocks.body:
What's NeverDestruct?

NeverDestruct brings a modifier-style and non destructive workflow to Blender. With its flagship Edit Poly modifier, every edits you make inside an Edit Poly layer is recorded, UVs, shapekeys, vertex groups, vertex colors and every topology changes, you do not need to use specific tools, everything is recorded, the addon constantly watches what happens to the object. Instead of commiting to your changes, you can now iterate directly on the object itself inside the modifier by using the journal system, which is a node based representation of your edits. You can create branches, edit past operations, mute or reroute. Once you're done editing, you can visualize everything you've done within that modifier.

On top of that, NeverDestruct brings more modifiers and tools, such as the Edit Mesh modifier which is a simplified and more straightforward version of Edit Poly, meant for higher density meshes, since every edits are local, you can still iterate changes through dedicated modifiers instead of the journal. You will also find a dedicated N panel with more tools, including smoothing groups, gizmo constraints and gizmo extrusion, more tools in the context menu and an overhauled modifier panel.

What's included:

-6 modifiers, Edit Poly, Edit Mesh, Weight Map, Shape Keys, FFD and Symmetry.

-General modifiers overhaul, with shared modifiers (shared between objects), copy and pasting modifiers, collapsable stack, dedicated UI for the new modifiers.

-Edit Poly tools in the N panel, including gizmo constraints (move, rotate and scale), smoothing groups and "caddy style" operations.

-Context menu tools, Align meshes (location, rotation and scale), ability to move the origin of an object directly, cloning more than once at a time, quick gizmo placement.

Requirements

Blender 5.2. Compatibility is not guaranteed on earlier versions.

Installation/Update

To install or update, find top left the Edit menu, then select “Preferences…”

Then go in “Get Extensions” and find the down arrow top right, then select ”Install from Disk…“

Then locate and select the downloaded NeverDestruct Zip file, and press “Install from Disk”

Base mesh and modifiers

The base mesh is your object's original mesh, this is the usual entry point for editing meshes in blender, it's evluated before any modifier.

Modifiers are evaluted on top of it, and always in the top -> bottom order.

Modifier types:

-Edit Poly: Record individual operations/steps, make branches, edit past values. Also record data like UV, Shapekeys, Vertex groups, Vertex colors.

-Edit Mesh: Store thre result. Iterate through individual modifiers. Also record data like UV, Shapekeys, Vertex groups, Vertex colors.

-FFD: Lattice wrapper with more controls, automatically fits the selection above it (Edit layers automatically create vertex groups of their selection), overhauled UI for easier back and forth editing.

-Symmetry: Mirror wrapper, automatically adds an empty, better UI controls as well, shortcuts button to automatically select the gizmo/visualize it, and go back and forth from the object -> symmetry gizmo.

-Shape Keys: Dedicated modifier to store Shape Keys.

-Weight Map: Dedicated modifier to store vertex groups.

Edit tools

Edit tools are accessible through any mean of editing, they're not exclusive to Edit Poly/Edit Mesh.

These tools use a "caddy" style editing, instead of selecting first then applying an edit, it allows you to select with the operation selected. This panel features either built-in operators or fully custom ones, for some tools, you can choose which implemnetation you use (blender vs custom).

Quick start with Edit Poly

Adding a layer: Select a mesh, open the modifier panel and choose add modifier -> Edit Poly

Edit it: Each modifier has a dedicated "active" button, for that active modifier, simply press tab, edit mode through the object modes or "edit" in the modifier itself to edit in that modifier.

Model: Model like usual, select faces, inset them, extrude the result, and go back to object mode. Edit Poly will store the individual operations.

Change the input: Set the base mesh active, edit at that layer, and start moving vertices around, once you're back in object mode, the edit poly will replay operations on that altered topology.

Open the Journal: In Edit Poly, at the very bottom you will find a button to open the Journal. Find the extrude node, and play with the values.

chapters.title: General overview of the modifier stack

blocks.body:
Basic interactions

You will find all the new modifiers directly in the add modifier panel, just like any regular modifier, they're displayed above the others as a quick way to access them. You're free to add any modifier anywhere you want in the stack, you're not limited in any way, nothing stays locked once you've begun editing, and no specific order is forced.

In addition to new modifiers, the addon adds a Base mesh layer as well that sits above all the modifiers. That layer represents the regular blender way to edit meshes.

Most new modifiers (such as Edit poly, Edit mesh, Shape keys or Weight Map) have a toggle to activate them, activating them allows you to interact with the mesh in this modifier specifically.

Editing the topology in a modifier that doesn’t support modifying it (such as Weight Map or Shape Keys) will automatically warn you that you are interacting in a layer that doesn’t support topology edits, your edits will not be stored.

Modifiers can be moved like you'd except for any regular modifier.

 

Base Mesh

This represents the most upstream mesh state, this is the default blender way, this modifies the mesh before any modifier. Since using the new modifiers is totally optional, you retain total access to modifying the mesh there. Applying modifiers will also push them to the base mesh layer, the base mesh becomes the mesh at the point you applied up to.

 

Edit Poly and Edit Mesh

Those are the mesh editing modifiers, however their use and features are different:

Edit poly is the modifier with the full replay system, the journal system, the safety features and it is the most non destructive modifier. Edit poly is capable of storing all changes, topology, uv edits, vertex groups, vertex colors and shapekeys, all are saved within that layer and editable at any point in time. It uses dedicated systems to keep edits as non destructive as possible. Edit poly features a full node based journal system that allows you to rewire, mute, edit values or reroute and create new branches, it allows for quick and efficient revisioning, editing the meshes in a simpler state, or very easily changing past operations (inset values, bevels, anything you do). On top of that, the edit poly modifier features safety mechanisms that prevent upstream edits, or journal revisioning to break final outputs, snapshots are stored of the last valid state for each branch output, this is also active if the addon fails for any case, and also can be enabled by the user manually.

Edit mesh is a lightweight mesh editing modifier, it retains some level of non destructiveness, but not to the extent of Edit poly. It doesn't use a replay system, no journal system, no branching and it has no safety mechanisms either, however it also saves UV, vertex groups, vertex colors and shapekeys. You can still revision, iterate using Edit mesh by using dedicated modifiers for your changes, but you cannot revision changes within that modifier, create branches, or edit operations within.

Both modifiers store their edits as relative to whatever is arriving in the modifier, meaning they're technically independent, nothing stops you from changing the topology above the layer, whether using another mesh editing modifier or anything else (geometry nodes, displacements...). The only exception is the snapshot safety system from Edit poly, this rightfully overrides incoming topology, as its purpose is a safety mechanism, it replaces it with the last valid mesh state.

Attributes such as shapekeys or vertex groups are also always added globally, because they sit outside the modifiers, and in order to keep it close to the native blender experience. The values/data is however defined per modifier.

Shape Keys and Weight Map

These are dedicated modifiers to purely save shape keys and weight map changes, no topology edits can be stored in these modifiers, attempting to make topology edits will display a warning and will discard your changes upon leaving edit mode.

Weight Map can store its data as relative or absolute, relative means that changes depend on the data it receives, for example, modifier 1 sets vertex 1's value to 0.5, modifier 2 bump it to 1, in relative mode, modifier 2 stores a +0.5 edit and is relative to anything it receives. Absolute on the other hand means that it disregards what it receives, vertex 1 is set to 1 in that modifier, nothing upstream can change that in this mode..

FFD and Symmetry

FFD is a wrapper for the lattice modifier already available in blender, it exists because it is meant to efficiently wrap around a selection automatically, using Edit Poly or Edit Mesh, you can select an area to create automatically a vertex group (or use your own vertex group), which can then be used in the FFD and automatically align it to the selection.

Symmetry is also a wrapper that automatically adds a gizmo, and adds visualization for the symmetry axis selected.

For both of these modifiers, you can enable the visibility of the lattice/gizmo by toggling on/off the most left button (eye icon), the button on the right of it allows you to instantly modify the lattice/gizmo, from the same modifier panel, you’re able to go back to the object, all seamlessly.

Stack interactions

The addon adds several new interactions with modifiers along the "activate" button, FFD and Symmetry have quick actions button allowing you to quickly view or edit them all through the stack.

Unlike regular blender, you are now able to instantly collapse the stack from a certain modifier using "apply up to", this allows all modifiers above that point to be applied. Base mesh then becomes that applied state, the stack still retains all modifiers that was sitting below that point. This is especially important because you can now work more iteratively in the stack, meaning you can stack up modifiers to arrive to a certain mesh state. You are still able to individually apply most modifiers, but edit poly for example only allows collapsing due to them depending on upstream topology.

The addon also add modifier instancing: one modifier on several objects. You can copy one modifier (in the regular drop down menu of any modifier) and paste it to your selection (in the add modifier panel, you will see an option to paste at the bottom), either as a copy or as an instance, when that modifier is an instance, settings are fully shared, you’re able to convert the modifier as “unique” at any point which will unlink the modifier.
